performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
intro: Fritz Reiner conducts the Pittsburgh Symphony in this 1946 recording of the first movement of the Concerto for Orchestra, Sz. 116, Introduzione — Andante non troppo; Allegro vivace. Cellos and basses climb through fourths, and later the brass play a fugue.

sections.label: Intro · Andante non troppo, cellos and basses
sections.mNote: Rising fourths beneath muted strings and flute figures.

sections.label: A · Violins launch the Allegro
sections.mNote: Quick violin phrases meet sharp wind and horn replies

sections.label: B · Oboe theme over string accompaniment
sections.mNote: Tranquillo: oboe, then clarinets, accompanied by horn and harp.

sections.label: Dev · Violins, trumpets, then woodwinds
sections.mNote: The opening figures rise through successive instrumental groups.

sections.label: Link · Clarinet and cor anglais
sections.mNote: Solo winds play above a few string parts

sections.label: Dev · Fugue begun by trombones
sections.mNote: Trombones and trumpets enter in turn, marked ben marcato.

sections.label: B′ · Tranquillo theme returns, clarinet
sections.mNote: The Tranquillo theme returns over strings and harp.

sections.label: A′ · Violins, first Allegro theme returns
sections.mNote: Strings accelerate and the first fast theme returns.

cues.title: Opening, cellos and double basses
cues.text: Cellos and double basses begin together, climbing in fourths. Muted violins enter above them, then a flute. The low phrase returns several times as more of the orchestra enters.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, plate B. & H. 9009, pp. 1–2: opening cello and bass phrase, divided muted violins and flute: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Emigration to America, 1940
cues.text: In October 1940 Bartók left Hungary for America. On the eve of leaving he wrote that the move was “like plunging into the unknown from what is known, but unbearable”. Columbia University gave him a modest research post in folk music for a number of months.
cues.evidence: Richard Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme note (17–19 January 2020), quoting Bartók on the eve of his departure and describing the Columbia post: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: Proposal for a commission, 1943
cues.text: In early 1943, when Bartók was ill and short of money, two old friends, the violinist Joseph Szigeti and the conductor Fritz Reiner, suggested to Serge Koussevitzky that he commission an orchestral work from him in memory of his wife, Natalie.
cues.evidence: Phillip Ramey’s account of the commission, quoted in Rodda’s Pittsburgh Symphony programme note: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: Koussevitzky’s commission, New York, 1943
cues.text: In 1943 Serge Koussevitzky visited Bartók in a New York hospital with a commission worth $1,000. At first Bartók accepted only half the money, because he feared his health would prevent him from finishing the piece. The work is dedicated to Koussevitzky’s late wife, Natalie.
cues.evidence: Richard E. Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme, January 2020, quoting Phillip Ramey’s account of the commission; the dedication is printed above the score’s first page: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf

cues.title: Allegro vivace, first theme
cues.text: Allegro vivace. The violins play a quick, twisting tune, and horns and bassoons reply beneath them. Oboes and clarinets add short, accented chords.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 5–8, Allegro vivace from bar 76: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bartók’s note on the title, 1944
cues.text: In his note for the Boston première in 1944, Bartók explained the title. The work treats single instruments or groups in a “concertant”, soloistic manner. His first example of this “virtuoso” treatment was the brass fugato in the development of this movement.
cues.evidence: Bartók’s note for the Boston première (1944), quoted in Rodda’s programme note, https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf, and in full by Brett Van Gansbeke, https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto (from Benjamin Suchoff, Bartók: Concerto for Orchestra, 1995).

cues.title: Oboe melody, Tranquillo, bar 155
cues.text: From bar 155 the oboe plays a new tune, marked dolce, over rocking figures in the violins and cellos. Muted horns hold the harmony. At bar 174 the clarinets take over the melody, and the harp plays between their phrases.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 9–11, Tranquillo from bar 155; clarinets take up the melody at bar 174: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Overlapping entries, bars 231–237
cues.text: The violins play the quick figure again. The trumpets follow, then bassoons and clarinets, then oboes and flutes. Each group enters before the previous one has finished.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 12, Tempo I, bars 231–237: successive string, trumpet and woodwind figures: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First commercial recording, Pittsburgh, 1946
cues.text: Reiner and the Pittsburgh Symphony made the first commercial recording of the Concerto on 4–5 February 1946, and it was issued in 1948. Reiner recorded the work again in Chicago for RCA on 22 October 1955.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments to the Henle edition, source RecR (recorded 4–5 February 1946; first commercial recording, issued 1948): https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf. Chicago Symphony Archives on the 22 October 1955 recording: https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/8311/125-moments-011-first-grammy-awards

cues.title: Tranquillo, clarinet and cor anglais
cues.text: At the Tranquillo (bar 272) the clarinet plays over violins and violas while most of the orchestra rests. The cor anglais takes over the line at bar 287, with a flute above it. The bass clarinet enters at bar 300.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 15–16, Tranquillo from bar 272, cor anglais from bar 287 and bass clarinet from bar 300: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brass fugato
cues.text: The trombones begin a fugato from bar 316, the same theme entering at different pitches before the earlier entries have finished. The trumpets then enter. Bartók marks the entries ben marcato.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 17–19: trombone fugato from bar 316, followed by trumpet entries, marked ben marcato. Bartók identifies this brass fugato in his première programme note: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf; https://www.orchestralbassoon.com/bartok-concerto
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation, second subject first
cues.text: After the brass passage ends, the clarinet brings back the Tranquillo tune over strings and harp. Bartók reversed the earlier order, so the lyrical tune returns before the fast violin theme.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 20–24: Tranquillo at bar 396, solo clarinet at bar 402, followed by the later return of the first group: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the first theme
cues.text: The strings accelerate and bring back the first fast theme. Below them, the horns repeat their short figure.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 24–28, accelerando from bar 476 and the closing first-group return: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The violins take over
transitions.from: Intro · Andante non troppo, cellos and basses
transitions.how: The introduction increases in speed over rising woodwind figures and a repeated phrase in the low strings. At bar 76, Allegro vivace, both violin sections take over the lead. Horns, bassoons and lower strings play accented notes in reply. Oboes and clarinets add short chords between the violin phrases.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 5, the approach to bar 76 and the opening Allegro vivace: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Oboe tune at Tranquillo
transitions.to: B · Oboe theme over string accompaniment
transitions.how: The tempo slows gradually to Tranquillo. The oboe begins a tune marked piano, dolce. First violins and cellos alternate between chords, two muted horns hold sustained notes above them, and the harp plays a short reply. The double basses rest.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 9, bars 149–174: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The quick figure moves upwards
transitions.from: B · Oboe theme over string accompaniment
transitions.how: At Tempo I (bars 231–237), unmuted violins bring back the quick figure above a timpani stroke. The trumpets then play it. Bassoons and clarinets enter together, followed by oboes and flutes, while horns, trombones and tuba hold a chord beneath the rising lines.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 12, bars 231–237: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Solo clarinet at Tranquillo
transitions.how: The orchestra broadens its last loud phrase, then stops. At Tranquillo, a solo clarinet plays the melody over first violins and violas, and the second violins join soon after. The cellos and double basses rest. The cor anglais later takes over the melody, with the flute above.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 15–16, bars 272–299: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Trombones enter one by one
transitions.how: The bass clarinet and strings slow down at the end of the quiet passage. At Tempo I the quick figure returns in the bassoons and low strings. The trombones then begin their overlapping entries, marked ben marcato. The trumpets join above them as the strings stop.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 16–17, bars 310–340: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Brass stop; clarinet enters at Tranquillo
transitions.how: The full orchestra broadens its repeated chords before Tranquillo. Strings and harp take over from the brass. Two horns put on mutes, and the clarinet enters with the lyrical tune, marked espressivo, above pizzicato double basses (bars 391–402).
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 20, bars 391–402: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The strings accelerate into the return
transitions.to: A′ · Violins, first Allegro theme returns
transitions.how: The wind figures thin out over repeated low-string notes. At the accelerando the violins remove their mutes and climb. The horns repeat a short figure with the cellos and basses, and the quick violin theme returns as the tempo increases.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 24–28, from bar 476: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, I
source.locator: Boosey & Hawkes full score, 1946, printed pp. 1–28: low-string introduction, wind solos, brass fugato and the returning violin theme.

timeline.note: Cellos and double basses climb together in fourths (p. 1).
Flute figures play above muted, divided strings (pp. 1–2).
Trumpet calls sound over moving violas, cellos and basses; horn and trombone hold notes behind them (pp. 2–4).
Quick violin phrases meet short woodwind and horn replies (pp. 5–8).
The oboe plays, then the clarinets, over rocking figures in the strings, horns and harp (pp. 9–11).
Clarinet, cor anglais and bass clarinet take turns with the quiet tune above strings (pp. 15–16).
Trombones and trumpets enter in turn in the fugato, with strings answering around them (pp. 17–19).
The clarinet brings back the lyrical tune over quiet strings, muted horns and harp (pp. 20–23).
The strings accelerate into the first fast tune, joined by winds and brass for the close (pp. 24–28).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: He saw a future for concert music in village songs and used a phonograph to record how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In May 1904 Bartók went to stay with the Fischer family at Gerlicepuszta. He had a piano sent out, practised four hours a day and composed for four or five more. There he heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania in the family’s service, singing to the children in her care, and began writing down her songs. Their Hungarian music differed from the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later the writer Béla Balázs went collecting with Bartók and recorded in his diary that the frail-looking pianist wore him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!”

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
